title: The Tiny Sandwich Secret
markdown:
Once upon a time, in a meadow painted with the brightest wildflowers and tickled by gentle breezes, lived a bunny named Thimble. He was as quick and bouncy as a summer shower, with long soft ears that twitched and swivelled at every new thought, and a twitchy little nose always ready for adventure. His very best friend in all the meadow was Jasper, a tortoise of immense patience and quiet wisdom. Jasper’s sturdy shell was the colour of old moss after a long rain. His steps were as slow and thoughtful as the changing of the seasons.

One particularly sunny morning, Thimble was practising his most impressive leaps near the old sundial. The sundial had stood in the meadow a very long time. Its stone face was worn smooth by many suns and rains. “Hup-two-three!” thumped Thimble, fluffy white tail bobbing like a happy dandelion seed. When he landed with a soft thump in the clover, he noticed something quite peculiar. Perched neatly on a smooth grey pebble right beside the sundial was a sandwich.

Not any sandwich. Tiny. No bigger than Thimble’s thumb. Two rounds of the softest bread, a sliver of bright lettuce peeking. His nose twitched. His ears stood. Who would leave such a thing?

“Jasper! Come quick!”

Jasper ambled over, kind eyes blinking. He peered. “Well now. That is indeed a curious sight.”

“Who made it? So small! So neat! Just right for a beetle!”

Jasper tilted his head, the way he did when thinking took the scenic route. “Perhaps a gift from meadow fairies. They enjoy little surprises, I’ve heard.”

Thimble giggled. “Or a secret from a very polite giant who knows how to make tiny perfect sandwiches.”

The next day, as if by appointment, another tiny sandwich waited. This one hid a crumb of bright red, like a jewel. They decided they must find the maker.

“We’ll watch,” Thimble declared, bouncing. “Behind the tall tickly grass. We won’t miss a thing.”

At rose-and-gold dawn they crept to the grass’s edge, eyes on the sundial. The sun climbed. Thimble’s paws warmed. Jasper’s shell took a pleasant heat. Thimble’s tummy rumbled — he had eaten clover, but tiny sandwiches made him peckish all over again. Jasper was still as stone.

A dazzling blue butterfly danced past Thimble’s nose. He hopped after its stained-glass wings. Jasper noticed a fat worm near his foot and leaned for a careful nibble. When they looked back, a new tiny sandwich sat as neat as the others.

“Oh, bother,” Thimble sighed. “We were looking the wrong way.”

This happened for several more days. One morning Thimble was captivated by a particularly interesting beetle, all shiny black armour, that scurried past with surprising speed. Another day Jasper was absorbed in a little red ladybird with seven black spots climbing a tall swaying blade of grass. Each time a tiny sandwich would appear. Each time they would be looking the wrong way, even for the briefest blink. The days passed with wonder and unanswered questions. The sundial kept its secret the way old stone does: by simply standing there.

Then, one quiet lazy afternoon, Thimble and Jasper sat near the sundial. They were not watching with the intense focused way they had been. They were just being, enjoying the peaceful hum of the meadow. The air was warm and thick with bees flitting from blossom to blossom. Thimble meticulously groomed his whiskers, making sure each one was in place. Jasper contemplated a particularly fluffy dandelion.

Thimble glanced at the sundial’s base. He froze. “Jasper. Look.”

A very small field mouse was not eating. It was working. From a larger, slightly crumbly sandwich in its paws it nipped delicate pieces and set them on the grey pebble, the way the others had been set. It was making many tiny sandwiches from its own large one.

It scurried, whiskers quivering, so focused it had not seen them.

Thimble and Jasper looked at each other. Not fairies. Not a polite giant. A resourceful mouse, sharing in portions for who-knew-who — ants, perhaps, or anyone who needed just a bite.

“It’s just sharing,” Thimble whispered. He had wanted a grand mystery. He had found a quiet kitchen.

Jasper nodded, slow. “Very good, when one has a little extra.”

Thimble’s nose twitched again, not with the old curiosity but with a brand-new idea. He hopped toward his cozy burrow and returned moments later, pushing with all his might the biggest, sweetest, juiciest carrot he could find. It was a magnificent carrot, far too big to finish in one sitting. Carefully he nudged the end close to the sundial, an offering for the busy mouse.

The mouse, finally noticing them, froze for a startled moment, bright eyes wide. Then it scampered a little closer, looking from the enormous carrot to Thimble and Jasper. It gave a tiny quick squeak that sounded remarkably like thank you, and began to explore the delicious unexpected orange.

After that, tiny sandwiches still appeared sometimes. Often, beside them, a pile of seeds or a ripe berry waited. Thimble left the carrot’s memory in the way he now sat still a little longer. Jasper watched the sundial’s shadow move, and did not mind missing a blink, now that he knew what the blinks had been for.
